claim: Achiasma in humans causes gross mis-wiring of the retinal-fugal projection, resulting in overlapped cortical representations of left and right visual hemifields.
source: Achiasma in humans causes gross mis-wiring of the retinal-fugal projection, resulting in overlapped cortical representations of left and right visual hemifields.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by the retinotopic mapping data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1) and citations to prior work on achiasma.

claim: In areas V1-V3, the overlap of visual field representations in achiasma is due to two co-located but non-interacting populations of neurons, each with a receptive field serving only one hemifield.
source: We show that in areas V1-V3 this overlap is due to two co-located but non-interacting populations of neurons, each with a receptive field serving only one hemifield.
evidence: This claim is supported by the adaptation experiments (Figure 2) and behavioral experiments (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) demonstrating independence of the two populations.

claim: The two neuronal populations in achiasmic visual cortex share the same local vascular control.
source: Importantly, the two populations share the same local vascular control, resulting in a unique organization useful for quantifying the relationship between neural and fMRI BOLD responses without direct measurement of neural activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization demonstrated by retinotopy and the BOLD summation results, combined with knowledge of neurovascular coupling.

claim: The amplitude of BOLD response is proportional to approximately 0.5 power of the underlying neural response.
source: Measurements from a series of such doubling experiments show that the amplitude of BOLD response is proportional to approximately 0.5 power of the underlying neural response.
evidence: This is directly supported by the BOLD summation experiments and stitching analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Most studies using the BOLD signal to infer brain activity rely on analytical methods that assume a linear relationship between the BOLD signal and neural response.
source: Most studies using the BOLD signal to infer brain activity rely on analytical methods (e.g., the general linear model) that assume a linear relationship between the BOLD signal and neural response, despite noticeable deviations from linearity (Boynton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, supported by citation to Boynton et al., 1996.

claim: The BOLD signal is indirectly related to local neural response through mechanisms associated with oxygen metabolism and blood flow.
source: The BOLD signal is indirectly related to local neural response through mechanisms associated with oxygen metabolism and blood flow (Davis et al., 1998; Hoge et al., 1999; Thompson et al., 2003; Griffeth and Buxton, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The achiasmic subject (S) was a 24-year-old Caucasian male diagnosed with isolated foveal hypoplasia.
source: Our primary research subject (S) was a 24-year-old achiasmic Caucasian male. S was diagnosed with isolated foveal hypoplasia.
evidence: This is a direct description of the subject from the Results section.

claim: The achiasmic subject's uncorrected visual acuity was 0.7 logMAR for the left eye and 0.5 logMAR for the right eye.
source: His uncorrected visual acuity was 0.7 logMAR for the left eye and 0.5 logMAR for the right eye (best-corrected 0.5 and 0.3 logMAR, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the Results section.

claim: The achiasmic subject has a congenital nystagmus with horizontal amplitude less than 2.1° (95 percentile).
source: He has a congenital nystagmus. His nystagmus (peak-to-peak) amplitude was less than 2.1° (95 percentile) horizontally and negligible (0.7°) vertically.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the Results section.

claim: The achiasmic subject's horizontal nystagmus followed a saw-tooth waveform with a right-forward fast phase and a frequency of between 0.6–2.3 Hz.
source: The horizontal nystagmus followed a saw-tooth waveform with a right-forward fast phase and a (horizontal) frequency of between 0.6–2.3 Hz (mode at 2.3 Hz) during tasks performed for the current study.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the Results section.

claim: The achiasmic subject was right-eye-preferred and suppressed his left eye.
source: He was right-eye-preferred and suppressed his left eye (self-report).
evidence: This is based on self-report from the subject.

claim: The achiasmic subject could not achieve binocular fusion and had no measurable stereoacuity.
source: He could not achieve binocular fusion and had no measurable stereoacuity.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the Results section.

claim: The absence of an optic chiasm in the achiasmic subject was confirmed using MRI.
source: We confirmed his absence of an optic chiasm using MRI (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: Within the retinotopically defined visual areas V1-V3, the achiasmic subject's retinotopic representation of the ipsilateral visual field is a mirror image of its contralateral field representation.
source: Within the retinotopically defined visual areas V1-V3, the subject's retinotopic representation of the ipsilateral visual field is a mirror image of its contralateral field representation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the retinotopic mapping data in Figure 1B.

claim: The two visual field representations are superimposed on the hemisphere ipsilateral to the stimulated eye in the achiasmic subject.
source: The two are superimposed on the hemisphere ipsilateral to the stimulated eye.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the retinotopic mapping in Figure 1B.

claim: Two points placed in the achiasmic subject's visual field symmetrically across the vertical meridian are mapped to the same point on the cortex.
source: Two points placed in the subject's visual field symmetrically across the vertical meridian are mapped to the same point on the cortex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the retinotopic mapping in Figure 1.

claim: The left-right mirror mapping in achiasma is established at the level of individual voxels (3x3x3 mm³).
source: This left-right mirror mapping is established at the level of individual voxels – 3x3x3 mm3 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C where individual voxel pRFs are plotted.

claim: Vertically-reflected stimuli showed nearly identical BOLD signal modulation for individual voxels in V1-V3 of the achiasmic subject.
source: Additional tests with vertically-reflected stimuli showed nearly identical BOLD signal modulation for individual voxels in V1-V3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The retinotopic findings in the achiasmic subject were consistent with previous reports on human achiasma.
source: These findings were consistent with previous reports on human achiasma (Hoffmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2012.

claim: The achiasmic subject does not show any behavioral confusion between visual hemifields.
source: Behaviorally, S does not show any confusion between visual hemifields.
evidence: This is an observation about the subject's behavior.

claim: The achiasmic subject is an avid reader, which strongly suggests that the co-localized neural populations do not interact functionally.
source: Most tellingly, S is an avid reader, which strongly suggests that the co-localized neural populations do not interact functionally (otherwise, the text on the left of fixation would mask the text on the right of fixation).
evidence: This is an inference based on the subject's reading ability and reasoning about what would happen if populations interacted.

claim: Placing a flickering checkerboard mask symmetrically across the vertical meridian from a target causes it to be projected to the same cortical location as the target in the achiasmic subject's visual cortex.
source: Placing the checkerboard mask symmetrically across the vertical meridian causes it to be projected to the same cortical location as the target in the visual cortex of S, while placing it across the horizontal meridian does not (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the retinotopic organization demonstrated in Figure 1 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The placement of a flickering checkerboard mask did not affect the contrast detection threshold in the achiasmic subject.
source: We found that the placement of the flickering checkerboard did not affect the detection threshold, and that the threshold is within the normal range without masking (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the psychophysical data in Figure 2B.

claim: Experiments have failed to demonstrate any anomalous interactions between the two pRFs in the achiasmic subject, strongly suggesting that the two underlying neural populations are functionally independent.
source: This and other experiments performed by us (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and others (Victor et al., 2000; Hoffmann and Dumoulin, 2015) have failed to demonstrate any anomalous interactions between the two pRFs, strongly suggesting that the two underlying neural populations are functionally independent.
evidence: This is based on multiple experiments (current study and cited studies) that failed to find interactions.

claim: Identical stimuli presented separately to either of the pRFs in the achiasmic subject yielded nearly identical BOLD responses.
source: We first established that identical stimuli presented separately to either of the pRFs yielded nearly identical BOLD responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the adaptors and test patterns were at the same spatial locations in the achiasmic subject, strong BOLD adaptation was observed when they were of matching orientation.
source: As expected, when the adaptors and test patterns were at the same spatial locations, we observed strong BOLD adaptation when they were of matching orientation and a large release from adaptation when they were of orthogonal orientations.
evidence: This is shown in the adaptation experiment results in Figure 2D.

claim: When adapting and testing patterns were at different spatial locations but projected to the same points on the cortex of the achiasmic subject, a large release from adaptation was observed regardless of orientation.
source: The critical conditions are when the adapting and testing patterns were at different spatial locations but projected to the same points on the cortex of S. In these conditions, regardless of orientation, we found a large release from adaptation equal or greater in amplitude than in the same-location cross-orientation condition.
evidence: This is shown in the adaptation experiment results in Figure 2D.

claim: The co-localized neural populations that underlie the two pRFs on either side of the vertical meridian in the achiasmic subject do not interact physiologically with each other.
source: We take this result to mean that the co-localized neural populations that underlie the two pRFs on either side of the vertical meridian do not interact physiologically with each other.
evidence: This is an inference from the adaptation experiment results.

claim: Each fMRI voxel in the visual cortex of the achiasmic subject contains two independent populations of neurons, each with a distinct pRF.
source: Our results thus far suggest that each fMRI voxel in the visual cortex of S contains two independent populations of neurons, each with a distinct pRF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the retinotopy, behavioral, and adaptation experiments.

claim: In V1-V3 and across contrast levels, the BOLD response to the combined stimulus A+B was significantly higher than what could be produced by doubling the contrast of stimulus A or B.
source: In V1-V3 and across the contrast levels, the BOLD response to the combined stimulus A+B was significantly higher than what could be produced by doubling the contrast of stimulus A or B [paired t-test; V1: t(19) = -4.48, p=2.57x10-4; V2: t(19) = -2.96, p=0.008; V3: t(19) = -4.30, p=3.85x10-4] (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is shown in the BOLD summation experiment results in Figure 3C with statistical tests.

claim: The BOLD response to the combined stimulus A+B was significantly lower than the sum of the BOLD responses to stimuli A and B.
source: but significantly lower than the sum of the BOLD responses to stimuli A and B [paired t-test; V1: t(24) = 2.53, p=0.018; V2: t(24) = 6.20, p=2.11x10-6; V3: t(24) = 6.07, p=2.87x10-6] (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the BOLD summation experiment results in Figure 3B with statistical tests.

claim: BOLD summation, in the absence of nonlinearity associated with neuronal summation, is itself nonlinear, with a compressive nonlinearity.
source: This finding shows that BOLD summation, in the absence of nonlinearity associated with neuronal summation (assuming that the A+B stimulus simultaneously excited two independent populations of neurons), is itself nonlinear, with a compressive nonlinearity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BOLD summation experiment results.

claim: The compressive nonlinearity in BOLD summation was not due to response saturation since the 1-s stimulation duration yielded essentially the same nonlinearity as the 6-s simulation.
source: The compressive nonlinearity was not due to response saturation since the 1-s stimulation duration yielded essentially the same nonlinearity as the 6-s simulation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results from 1-s and 6-s stimulus durations.

claim: The BOLD summation results imply a nonlinear relationship between neural and BOLD responses, and challenge the prevailing linearity assumption.
source: This result implies a nonlinear relationship between neural and BOLD responses, and challenges the prevailing linearity assumption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BOLD summation experiment results.

claim: For a stimulus duration of 6 s, the exponent γ of the BvZ function was 0.76 [95% CI: 0.66, 0.87], 0.54 [0.48, 0.62], and 0.55 [0.46, 0.67] for V1, V2, and V3, respectively.
source: We found that for a stimulus duration of 6 s, γ = 0.76 [95% CI: 0.66, 0.87], 0.54 [0.48, 0.62], and 0.55 [0.46, 0.67] for V1, V2, and V3, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct result from the stitching analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The exponents γ were statistically indistinguishable between V2 and V3 for the 6-s stimulus.
source: The exponents were indeed statistically indistinguishable between V2 and V3; however, the value for V1 was outside the 95% confidence intervals of the values for V2 and V3 and vice versa (Figure 4C, left column).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The measured γ value obtained in V1 was inflated towards unity (linearity) because the neural populations associated with the two pRFs are not truly co-localized in V1.
source: We believe that the measured γ value obtained in V1 was inflated towards unity (linearity) because the neural populations associated with the two pRFs are not truly co-localized in V1 (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the V1 results based on reasoning about cortical organization.

claim: Combining the measurements from areas V2 and V3 yields a BvZ function with an exponent equal to 0.54 ± 0.05 for the 6-s stimulus.
source: We thus combine the measurements from areas V2 and V3 to obtain the BvZ function with an exponent equal to 0.54 ± 0.05 for the 6-s stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct result from combining V2 and V3 data.

claim: Reducing the stimulus duration from 6 s to 1 s resulted in only small changes to the exponent of the BvZ function, with γ = 0.56 [0.51,0.62], 0.49 [0.44,0.54], and 0.43 [0.37,0.50] for V1, V2, and V3, respectively.
source: Reducing the stimulus duration from 6 s to 1 s resulted in only small changes to the exponent of the BvZ function, with γ = 0.56 [0.51,0.62], 0.49 [0.44,0.54], and 0.43 [0.37,0.50] for V1, V2, and V3, respectively (Figure 4, right column).
evidence: This is a direct result from the stitching analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Combining data from V2 and V3 for the 1-s stimulus yields γ = 0.47 ± 0.03.
source: Combining data from V2 and V3 yield γ = 0.47 ± 0.03.
evidence: This is a direct result from combining V2 and V3 data for the 1-s stimulus.

claim: A sixfold change in stimulus duration resulted in very little change in the nonlinearity of the BvZ function.
source: Hence, a sixfold change in stimulus duration resulted in very little change in the nonlinearity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the γ values for 1-s and 6-s stimuli.

claim: Combining data from the two stimulus durations yields γ ~ 0.5.
source: Combining data from the two stimulus durations, we have γ ~ 0.5.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from both stimulus durations.

claim: The inferred neural activity in V1 for both the 6-s and 1-s stimuli matched extremely well with the average primate V1 contrast response function measured in terms of single-unit spiking activity by Albrecht (1995).
source: The inferred neural activity in V1 for both the 6-s and 1-s stimuli matched extremely well with the average primate V1 contrast response function measured in terms of single-unit spiking activity by Albrecht (1995) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A where the inferred neural responses are compared to single-unit data.

claim: Linearly scaling BOLD amplitude data does not fit the single-unit spiking data from Albrecht (1995).
source: Contrary to earlier reports based on the same single-unit data (Heeger et al., 2000), linearly scaling our BOLD amplitude data does not fit the single-unit spiking data.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A where linearly scaled BOLD data does not match single-unit data.

claim: The nonlinearity in the BOLD data cannot be attributed to anticipatory and other endogenous responses that might be induced by the task structure.
source: The nonlinearity in our data cannot be attributed to anticipatory and other endogenous responses that might be induced by the task structure (Sirotin and Das, 2009) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the lack of response in the left hemisphere (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and the task design.

claim: The subject was engaged in a demanding central fixation task (orientation discrimination) that was asynchronous with the blocked contrast stimuli.
source: This is because our subject was engaged in a demanding central fixation task (orientation discrimination) that was asynchronous with the blocked contrast stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The BvZ function obtained from the achiasmic subject, with γ~0.5, appears to represent the typical neurovascular coupling in humans.
source: The BvZ function obtained from our achiasmic subject, with γ~0.5, appears to represent the typical neurovascular coupling in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the meta-analysis of 21 datasets from 12 published studies.

claim: The bulk of the distribution of γ from the meta-analysis lies mid-range between 0 and 1.
source: With respect to the two neuronal contrast response functions, the bulk of the distribution of γ lies mid-range between 0 and 1 (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is shown in the histograms in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: The interquartile range of both distributions from the meta-analysis includes γ ~ 0.5.
source: The interquartile range of both distributions includes γ ~ 0.5, the exponent of the BvZ function independently estimated from our pure BOLD summation experiments with subject S.
evidence: This is shown in the histograms in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: γ ~ 0.5 is near the median of one distribution and the mode of the other distribution from the meta-analysis.
source: In fact, γ ~ 0.5 is near the median of one distribution (Figure 5C) and the mode of the other distribution (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in the histograms in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: Williams et al. (1994) found that in achiasmic Belgian sheepdogs, retinal axons originating from the nasal hemi-retina innervated ipsilateral LGN and occupied those layers that would otherwise receive inputs from the contralateral eye.
source: Williams et al. (1994) found that in achiasmic Belgian sheepdogs, retinal axons originating from the nasal hemi-retina, which would normally cross the midline, instead innervated ipsilateral LGN and occupied those layers that would otherwise receive inputs from the contralateral eye.
evidence: This is a citation to Williams et al. (1994).

claim: Alternating layers of the LGN in achiasma form mirror-image maps of the visual field.
source: Alternating layers of the LGN in achiasma thus form mirror-image maps of the visual field.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings from Williams et al. (1994).

claim: If axon guidance between LGN and V1 during development is typical in achiasma, then what would develop into the ocular dominance columns of V1 in a normal visual system will instead become visual-field dominance columns in achiasma.
source: If axon guidance between LGN and V1 during development is typical in achiasma, then what would develop into the ocular dominance columns of V1 in a normal visual system will instead become visual-field dominance columns in achiasma, as suggested by Victor et al. (2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about development and cited work by Victor et al. (2000).

claim: Preliminary measurements with 7T fMRI showed results consistent with the presence of visual-field dominance columns in V1.
source: Preliminary measurements with 7T fMRI showed results consistent with the presence of visual-field dominance columns in V1 (Olman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olman et al., 2014.

claim: The organization of visual-field dominance columns is expected to be mostly within Layer 4 of V1, which receives direct hemifield-segregated inputs from LGN.
source: We expect the organization of visual-field dominance columns to be mostly within Layer 4 of V1, which receives direct hemifield-segregated inputs from LGN (Williams et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on knowledge of cortical organization and cited work.

claim: Downstream from Layer 4, the columnar organization is expected to dissolve into finely intermingled but non-interacting unilateral (and monocular) neurons.
source: Downstream from Layer 4, we expect this columnar organization to dissolve into finely intermingled but non-interacting unilateral (and monocular) neurons, for the following reason.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about cortical organization.

claim: In achiasma, 'binocular' neurons would stay monocular and unilateral because the inputs from neighboring visual-field dominance columns would not correlate.
source: However, in achiasma, such 'binocular' neurons would stay monocular and unilateral. This is because the inputs from neighboring visual-field dominance columns would not correlate, as they represent unrelated locations in the left and right visual fields.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about neural development and connectivity.

claim: Neurons that received inputs from neighboring columns would likely suppress or eliminate the inputs from one of the visual fields, chosen at random and without preference.
source: Neurons that received inputs from neighboring columns would likely suppress or eliminate the inputs from one of the visual fields, chosen at random and without preference, since the inputs from the two visual fields are of equal strength (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about neural competition and supported by data showing equal strength inputs.

claim: Downstream from Layer 4 of V1, neurons that represented different hemifields of the visual space would be functionally independent but finely intermingled.
source: Hence, downstream from Layer 4 of V1, neurons that represented different hemifields of the visual space would be functionally independent but finely intermingled.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about cortical organization.

claim: There is a coarse segregation, at the scale of the ocular dominance columns, of the unilateral neuronal populations in Layer 4 of V1.
source: In other words, we speculate a coarse segregation, at the scale of the ocular dominance columns, of the unilateral neuronal populations in Layer 4 of V1.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The intermixing of the unilateral neurons would become finer downstream from V1 Layer 4, starting with neurons in the superficial and deep layers of V1.
source: The intermixing of the unilateral neurons would become finer downstream from V1 Layer 4, starting with neurons in the superficial and deep layers of V1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about cortical organization.

claim: The coarsely segregated neuronal populations in V1 Layer 4, which would not fully share the local vascular system, lead to a more linear summation (higher value of γ).
source: This may explain why the γ value of the BvZ function observed in V1 was higher than those found in V2 and V3 – the coarsely segregated neuronal populations in V1 Layer 4, which would not fully share the local vascular system, lead to a more linear summation (higher value of γ).
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed difference in γ values.

claim: In V1, Layer 4 tends to have a larger contribution to the measured BOLD signal because of its dense vasculature but contributions from superficial and deep layers are also significant.
source: In V1, Layer 4 tends to have a larger contribution to the measured BOLD signal because of its dense vasculature but contributions from superficial and deep layers are also significant (Polimeni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Polimeni et al., 2010.

claim: Neurons representing the two hemifields would likely be more intermingled in the superficial and deep layers than those in Layer 4.
source: We postulate that neurons representing the two hemifields would be more intermingled in the superficial and deep layers than those in Layer 4.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a postulate.

claim: Neurons in superficial and deep layers of V1 would likely be more complex and less linear in their response properties to visual stimulation than neurons in Layer 4.
source: These neurons would likely be more complex and less linear in their response properties to visual stimulation than neurons in Layer 4 (Movshon et al., 1978a,b).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of cortical organization and cited work.

claim: The contribution of superficial and deep layer neurons to the BOLD signal relative to those in Layer 4 may be significantly reduced with long-duration simulation because of adaptation.
source: Their contribution to the BOLD signal relative to those in Layer 4 may be significantly reduced with long-duration simulation because of adaptation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the difference between 1-s and 6-s conditions.

claim: The summation function cannot be used to infer the BvZ function if the conditions of co-localization and non-interaction are not met.
source: It is important to point out that the summation function cannot be used to infer the BvZ function if the conditions of co-localization and non-interaction are not met.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the requirements for the inference method.

claim: The condition of co-localization was not met in V1, and the summation function of V1 could not be used to infer its BvZ function.
source: The condition of co-localization was not met in V1, and we could not use the summation function of V1 to infer its BvZ function.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the applicability of the method to V1.

claim: The relationship between neural and BOLD responses does not depend significantly on stimulus duration.
source: We do not think that the relationship between neural and BOLD responses depends significantly on stimulus duration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similarity of γ values for different stimulus durations.

claim: The BvZ functions inferred from V2 and V3 provide an excellent fit to the V1 single-unit data, suggesting that the inferred BvZ function is applicable in at least V1-V3.
source: The fact that the BvZ functions inferred from V2 and V3, where the co-localization condition was met, provides an excellent fit to the V1 single-unit data (Figure 5A) further suggests that the inferred BvZ function is applicable in at least V1-V3.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cross-validation with single-unit data.

claim: The unique organization of the low-level visual cortex in human achiasma provides a versatile in vivo model for non-invasive quantification of the relationship between the evoked neural and fMRI BOLD responses.
source: We have shown that the unique organization of the low-level visual cortex in human achiasma provides a versatile in vivo model for non-invasive quantification of the relationship between the evoked neural and fMRI BOLD responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: By measuring the fMRI BOLD responses associated with a doubling of the local neural response, the amplitude of the evoked BOLD response is proportional to the sum-total of the evoked neural response raised to a power around 0.5.
source: By measuring the fMRI BOLD responses associated with a doubling of the local neural response, we found that the amplitude of the evoked BOLD response is proportional to the sum-total of the evoked neural response raised to a power around 0.5.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the BOLD summation experiments and analysis.

claim: Reported cases of achiasma in the scientific literature are rare, particularly with regards to fMRI studies.
source: Reported cases of achiasma in the scientific literature are rare, particularly with regards to fMRI studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature on achiasma.

claim: Victor et al. (2000) performed a seminal study on the achiasmic visual system, the first one using fMRI and with a single subject.
source: Victor et al. (2000) performed a seminal study on the achiasmic visual system, the first one using fMRI and with a single subject.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: A more recent fMRI study on achiasma was conducted by Hoffmann et al. (2012) with two subjects, one in Germany and the other in the US.
source: A more recent fMRI study, which provided a detailed characterization of the cortical representations of visual fields in achiasma, was conducted by Hoffmann et al. (2012) with two subjects, one in Germany and the other in the US.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Another recent fMRI study on the achiasmic visual pathway was conducted by Davies-Thompson et al. (2013) with a single subject.
source: Another recent fMRI study on the achiasmic visual pathway was conducted by Davies-Thompson et al. (2013) with a single subject.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: None of the prior fMRI studies on achiasma attempted to use achiasma as a model system to study the relationship between neural response and the BOLD signal.
source: None of these studies attempted to use achiasma as a model system to study the relationship between neural response and the BOLD signal, nor had they thoroughly assessed the neural underpinning of the overlapped visual-field representations in achiasma.
evidence: This is a statement about the prior literature.

claim: The fMRI visual field mapping results from prior studies on achiasma are very similar to the results from the current study, suggesting that the current subject is a 'typical' achiasmic individual.
source: Nevertheless, the fMRI visual field mapping results from these prior studies are very similar to our results, suggesting that our subject is a 'typical' achiasmic individual.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work to establish generalizability.

claim: Among the rare achiasmic patient population, the current subject was unique in being otherwise neurologically normal and very dedicated to the research.
source: Yet, among this rare patient population, our subject was unique. Aside from being otherwise neurologically normal, he was very dedicated to this research and made himself available for nearly a year to complete a large set of converging experiments, including replications.
evidence: This is a description of the subject.

claim: The meta-analysis of published data from neurologically normal participants was hypothesis-driven, based on results from the achiasmic subject.
source: This meta-analysis was hypothesis-driven, based on results from our achaismic subject.
evidence: This is a description of the meta-analysis approach.

claim: The meta-analysis found that the exponent γ is around 0.5, in agreement with findings from the single achiasmic subject.
source: Our meta-analysis found that the exponent is around 0.5, in agreement with our findings from the single achiasmic subject.
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis shown in Figure 5.
